![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212195/assets/8036801735554767a33bdee0ff96a95d7e44bc3f97bacb396ec0de6d38f4aafc.png)

A cone is being filled with ice-cream at a rate of $4\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/s}.$ The height of the cone is always three times its base radius. At what rate is the radius of the ice cream volume increasing when the radius is $1\,\text{cm}?$
question.worked_solution:
Let's call $h$ the height of the ice cream volume and $r$ the radius of its base. Both of these quantities, as well as the volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=1\,\text{cm}.$

We need to find a relation between $h$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $v.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $h$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $h$ in terms of $r.$

We're told that the height is always three times its base diameter. So, we have $h=3r.$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}(3r) \\  & =\pi {r}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $r,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{3}) \\  & =3\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting the known values and solving for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =3\pi (1)^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\ 4 & =3\pi \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{4}{3\pi }\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$
